column5: Moses, fire, and not being consumed
column6: Exodus makes the burning bush blaze without being consumed; it supplies the same Moses-and-fire encounter against which the commentary distinguishes Moses receiving guidance near fire from the wretched person entering fire in 87:12–13.

column5: Distant fire becoming a path
column6: Moses turns aside to inspect the blazing bush, giving a narrative counterpart to the commentary's distant fire that draws him into a way of guidance.

column5: God's call from the bush
column6: God calls Moses from the bush when he comes near; this is the fire-side encounter behind the commentary's sequence of fire, choice, and address.

column5: Moses chosen and sent against Pharaoh
column6: At the bush God sends Moses to bring Israel from Egypt, a direct counterpart to the commentary's election at the fire and its later Pharaoh scene.

column5: Fire-side commission issuing in worship
column6: God's sign to the commissioned Moses is that Israel will worship God at the mountain, supplying a biblical fire-to-worship movement beside the commentary's prayer after election.

column5: Q20:14 li-dhikri and Hebrew zikhri
column6: At the bush the revealed name is God's perpetual memorial, Hebrew zikhri; its Semitic cognate relation to the commentary's li-dhikri joins divine name and remembrance at the same Moses encounter.

column5: Fire that leads by the way
column6: The night pillar of fire gives Israel light in order to travel, a concrete biblical meeting of fire, path, and divine guidance rather than fire as punishment.

column5: Stephen's flame in the bush
column6: Acts explicitly retells an angel appearing to Moses in a flame of a bush in the wilderness, preserving the scene around which the commentary gathers call and guidance.

column5: The bush appearance and Moses's sending
column6: Stephen calls Moses the man sent by God as ruler and deliverer through the angel who appeared in the bush; it joins election at the fire to opposition from Egypt.

column5: The book of Moses at the bush
column6: Jesus identifies the bush episode as a passage in the book of Moses, directly joining the commentary's final Moses pages to its opening fire encounter.

column5: Pharaoh's Egyptian sorcerers
column6: Pharaoh summons wise men and sorcerers to meet Moses, the Torah's direct setting for the commentary's later gathering of Moses, Pharaoh, and magicians.

column5: Competing staffs and Aaron's victory
column6: The magicians' staffs become serpents but Aaron's staff swallows them; this supplies the contest which the commentary reads through the magicians' eventual refusal of Pharaoh.

column5: Magicians acknowledge God's agency
column6: When their art fails, the Egyptian magicians tell Pharaoh that the plague is God's finger; their recognition is a biblical counterpart to the commentary's magicians breaking with Pharaoh's claim.

column5: Egyptian magic publicly disgraced
column6: Wisdom presents the Egyptian magic arts as shamed during the plague darkness, a Jewish expansion of the Moses-versus-magicians setting that makes magical competence fail before God's act.

column5: Jannes and Jambres oppose Moses
column6: The letter gives traditional names to men who opposed Moses, a Christian reception of the Egyptian-magician conflict that the commentary brings into the Pharaoh scene.

column5: Refusal to worship under a king's fire threat
column6: The Judeans refuse the king's gods even when a furnace is threatened; the scene closely meets the commentary's prostrating magicians who reject a tyrant's finite authority.

column5: Entrants into fire who are unharmed
column6: The king sees the furnace's entrants walking unhurt; its outcome stands in deliberate tension with the commentary's person who enters the great fire and neither dies nor lives.

column5: A ruler's limited power over life
column6: Jesus distinguishes people who can kill only the body from God who judges finally; this clarifies the commentary's assertion that Pharaoh rules only this worldly life while God is more enduring.

column5: Moses refuses Pharaoh's household
column6: Moses refuses the status of Pharaoh's daughter's son, a specific Christian reading of the choice the commentary places beside Pharaoh's transient rule.

column5: Choosing suffering over passing pleasure
column6: Moses chooses ill-treatment with God's people rather than sin's temporary enjoyment, closely matching the commentary's preference between the near worldly life and what lasts.

column5: Egyptian treasure weighed against a future reward
column6: Moses values reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looks to recompense; the verse gives the commentary's choice and permanence an explicitly Mosaic Christian form.

column5: A tyrant ends present life, God raises to lasting life
column6: A tortured brother tells the king that he may dismiss them from present life but the King of the world will raise them to everlasting life, closely meeting Pharaoh's threat and the better enduring life.

column5: Mortal death and resurrection unto life
column6: Another brother contrasts death at human hands with hope of resurrection and tells the tyrant he has no resurrection to life; it is a pointed counter-formulation to neither dying nor living in the fire.

column5: A governor's brief fire and future judgment
column6: Polycarp answers a ruler's fire threat by contrasting a short-lived flame with future judgment; the martyr tradition sharpens the commentary's contrast between Pharaoh's claimed lasting punishment and divine permanence.

column5: The Most High gives kingdoms to whom he wills
column6: Daniel says the Most High rules human kingdoms and gives them as he chooses, directly contesting Pharaoh's self-exalting authority and joining highness to election.

column5: A humbled king praises the Most High
column6: After his humiliation, the king blesses and honors the Most High whose dominion endures; it reverses the commentary's tyrannical high claim with praise and lasting rule.

column5: Undying worm and unquenched fire
column6: Isaiah's final spectacle of the unquenched fire and worm that does not die is a close Hebrew-Bible horizon for the commentary's great fire and suspended death-life.

column5: Christian citation of undying worm and unquenched fire
column6: Mark preserves Isaiah's image for Gehenna, making an explicit Christian counterpart to the commentary's fire in which ordinary death does not bring release.

column5: People seek death but death flees
column6: In Revelation's torment people long to die yet cannot find death; this is a particularly close formulation beside the commentary's neither-dying-nor-living fire.

column5: Furnace as testing rather than annihilation
column6: The furnace tests silver and gold while God tests hearts, supplying the corrective operation of fire that the commentary sets beside fire as punishment.

column5: Refining and purifying through fire
column6: The divine messenger sits as a refiner and purifier of silver; this gives a biblical analogue for the commentary's distinction between a fire that sets something right and a fire endured as ruin.

column5: Dross removed so silver becomes usable
column6: Removing dross from silver leaves material for the smith, a precise counterpart to the commentary's furnace foam: what is waste departs while what is useful remains.

column5: Gold tested in fire and the righteous in humiliation
column6: Sirach's fire-testing of gold supplies a Jewish wisdom formulation for the commentary's corrective fire, without making it identical to the punitive fire.

column5: Fire tests the quality of each work
column6: Paul's fire reveals whether work endures, directly extending the commentary's fire, useful remainder, and lasting good into a Christian assessment of works.

column5: Saved as through fire
column6: Paul can describe a person whose work burns yet who is saved through fire; that different result makes a useful counterpoint to the commentary's condemned person inside the great fire.

column5: Waters apportioned by measure
column6: Job says God established weight for wind and measured the waters, closely meeting the commentary's flood running in valleys according to measure.

column5: God measures the waters and creation
column6: Isaiah pictures God measuring waters in his hand and the cosmos by span, expanding the commentary's measuring scene from floodwater to ordered creation.

column5: All things arranged by measure, number, and weight
column6: This Jewish wisdom formula directly parallels the commentary's repeated movement from measured water to a created order apportioned by God.

column5: Rain makes earth sprout and yield
column6: Rain descends, waters the earth, and makes it bear seed and bread; it is the biblical side of the commentary's rain, pasture, cultivated field, and beneficial yield.

column5: Rain makes grass sprout in waste ground
column6: God's rain satisfies desolate ground and causes grass to spring up, a precise meeting of the commentary's rain-shaken earth and brought-forth pasture.

column5: God causes grass and cultivated vegetation to grow
column6: The psalm distinguishes grass for animals and vegetation for human cultivation, furnishing a close biblical landscape for the commentary's pasture and worked soil.

column5: Fruitful tree by streams that does not wither
column6: The water-planted tree bears fruit and does not wither, concretely supplies the commentary's useful, enduring side of water and vegetation.

column5: Chaff driven away
column6: The wicked are wind-driven chaff, a biblical residue image beside the commentary's flood-carried foam and dried pasture that do not remain.

column5: Roaring waters and dispersed chaff
column6: Nations roar like waters but flee like chaff before wind; this joins rushing flood imagery to transient residue as the commentary does.

column5: Floodwater washes away earth
column6: Water wears stone and sweeps away soil, a literal counterpart to the commentary's flood carrying off what has dried and become refuse.

column5: Grass withers and flower fades
column6: Isaiah's grass and flower wither under divine breath, giving a close biblical form to the commentary's worldly life becoming dried pasture.

column5: God's word stands forever after grass withers
column6: The word's permanence is set directly against withering grass, completing the commentary's contrast between transient vegetation and what remains.

column5: All flesh as grass
column6: First Peter reapplies the grass-and-fading-flower image to mortal human life, a Christian articulation of the commentary's worldly-life-as-grass scene.

column5: The word remains forever
column6: The citation's next verse makes the Lord's word endure forever, matching the commentary's passage from drying life to an enduring word and future.

column5: Rain-drinking ground that yields a useful crop
column6: Ground receives rain and produces a crop useful to its cultivators, a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's worked field that grows and remains beneficial.

column5: Thorny ground ending in burning
column6: Ground producing thorns is rejected and ends in burning; it gives the commentary's neglected weed, field, and fire a sharply opposed agricultural outcome.

column5: Break fallow ground and do not sow among thorns
column6: Jeremiah turns cultivation into moral exhortation, making a direct Jewish parallel for the commentary's ploughed field versus vegetation left to become waste.

column5: Sow righteousness and break fallow ground
column6: Hosea links cultivated ground, righteousness, and a coming divine response, a close ethical field analogue to the commentary's falah-like salvation and lasting crop.

column5: Prepared vineyard yielding wild grapes
column6: The carefully cultivated vineyard gives wild fruit instead of the expected crop; it adds a prophetic moral version of the commentary's contrast between worked land and uncontrolled growth.

column5: A harvested sheaf deliberately left for others
column6: The forgotten sheaf must remain for the resident alien, orphan, and widow, concretely illuminating the commentary's claim that a field's produce has a due share left behind.

column5: Sowing for decay or eternal life
column6: Sowing to flesh reaps corruption while sowing to Spirit reaps eternal life, translating the commentary's worldly and afterlife fields into a moral agricultural choice.

column5: Doing good and reaping in due season
column6: The promise that persistent good will reap at the proper time supplies a Christian counterpart to the commentary's lasting good that remains after the transient growth goes.

column5: Wheat gathered and weeds burned
column6: The parable preserves wheat while gathering weeds for burning, closely pairing the commentary's useful field, rejected vegetation, division, and fire.

column5: Unfruitful branch dries and is thrown into fire
column6: A branch not abiding is dried, gathered, and burned, a concentrated Christian image for the commentary's dried vegetation and fire-bound outcome.

column5: Human body formed from earth
column6: God forms the human from ground and breathes life into it, furnishing the body-and-earth side of the commentary's creating and fashioning pair.

column5: Skin, flesh, bones, and sinews fashioned
column6: Job describes God clothing and knitting the body, a concrete biblical counterpart to the commentary's secondary sense of bodily and embryonic formation.

column5: Formed in the womb and appointed
column6: Before forming Jeremiah in the womb God knows, consecrates, and appoints him; it joins formation, election, and a divine mission as the commentary does at Moses's fire.

column5: Maker from the womb who has chosen
column6: Isaiah calls God the maker and former from the womb and names the chosen servant, an unusually close pairing for the commentary's crafted body and selection.

column5: A mortal shaped in a mother's womb
column6: Wisdom describes ordinary human formation in the womb from earthly mortality, a Jewish literary counterpart to the commentary's womb-to-earth connection.

column5: The servant made a polished arrow
column6: Isaiah's servant is made into a polished arrow and kept hidden; this supplies the crafted-arrow secondary sense which the commentary finds in the creation verb.

column5: Clay, potter, and work of God's hand
column6: The potter-clay image gives the commentary's craft language a biblical body-and-maker analogy without reducing it to a lexical echo.

column5: Set apart from the womb and called
column6: Paul describes being set apart from his mother's womb and called by grace, a Christian counterpart to formed life that is also chosen for a task.

column5: Potter's authority over clay vessels
column6: Paul uses a potter making vessels for different purposes, joining divine fashioning to differentiated allotment in the way the commentary connects creation and choice.

column5: God guides the blind on an unknown path
column6: God leads blind people on paths they do not know and turns darkness into light, a close biblical formulation for the commentary's measure-then-guidance and fire-path scene.

column5: God's just scales and weights
column6: The proverb makes weights and measures God's work, supporting the commentary's secondary move from cosmic measuring to a just apportioned share.

column5: Cleansing from impurities and idols
column6: God sprinkles clean water, cleanses Israel, and removes its idols, giving the commentary's purification and Abrahamic distance from idolatry a single biblical cleansing horizon.

column5: Proclaiming the divine name and ascribing greatness
column6: Moses announces that he will proclaim YHWH's name and ascribe greatness to God, a close Torah counterpart to the commentary's praise of the exalted Lord and mention of the name.

column5: The exalted name alone praised
column6: The psalm calls for praise of YHWH's name because that name alone is exalted above earth and heaven, closely meeting the commentary's name, praise, and highness.

column5: Abraham invokes El Elyon, God Most High
column6: Abraham names YHWH El Elyon, God Most High; Hebrew elyon and the commentary's al-Ala share the highness root and join the title to Abraham named in 87:19.

column5: The high and lofty one revives the lowly
column6: The high and lofty God dwells with the contrite in order to revive them, pairing the commentary's highness with its purified, responsive person rather than the arrogant ruler.

column5: Prayer that hallows God's name
column6: The opening petition of the Lord's Prayer hallows the Father's name, an explicit Christian prayer counterpart to the commentary's remembering the Lord's name and praying.

column5: Secret things and revealed obligations
column6: The secret belongs to God while what is revealed is for communal obedience, a precise Torah counterpart to the commentary's hidden divine matter and disclosed teaching.

column5: God knows and reveals hidden things
column6: Daniel says God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness, closely meeting the commentary's God who knows what is open and concealed.

column5: Do not forget the revelation and teach it
column6: Israel must guard itself from forgetting what it saw and make it known to children, directly paralleling the commentary's word gathered, not forgotten, and offered as reminder.

column5: Write and teach the song as a witness
column6: God tells Moses to write a song, teach it, and put it in Israel's mouths; it supplies a Mosaic written-and-remembered form for the commentary's recitation and warning.

column5: A song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
column6: The divinely given song will not be forgotten from descendants, a particularly close biblical analogue to the commentary's not-forgetting and enduring instruction.

column5: Book in the mouth and continual meditation
column6: Joshua is told not to let the Torah book depart from his mouth but to meditate on it day and night, matching the commentary's preserved speech, remembrance, and practice.

column5: Forgetting a word of study
column6: The Mishnah applies Deuteronomy's warning to the deliberate forgetting of a learned word; it is a Jewish interpretive intensification of the commentary's not-forgetting motif.

column5: Not a forgetful hearer but a doer
column6: James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the persevering doer of the perfect law, directly pairing the commentary's reminder with its division between response and avoidance.

column5: Life and good set against death and evil
column6: Moses sets life and good before Israel against death and evil, a Torah form of the two human outcomes the commentary traces from reminder through fire and purification.

column5: Choose life
column6: The call to choose life gives explicit Mosaic form to the commentary's language of preference and its contrast between the near life and what truly endures.

column5: Everlasting life and everlasting abhorrence
column6: Daniel's awakening divides people between everlasting life and enduring disgrace, furnishing a biblical future horizon for the commentary's high ranks and great fire.

column5: This world as corridor before the world to come
column6: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the world to come, a precise rabbinic frame for the commentary's worldly life versus the later, enduring life.

column5: Good deeds here and bliss in the world to come
column6: The saying weighs repentance and good deeds in this world together with the incomparable bliss of the world to come, closely mapping the commentary's earthly choice and better permanence.

column5: Seen things temporary and unseen things eternal
column6: Paul explicitly contrasts the temporary visible with the eternal unseen, giving the commentary's dunya-versus-lasting formulation a close Christian analogue.

column5: The world passes, the doer remains
column6: The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, directly matching the commentary's transient life and lasting good.

column5: Eternal punishment and eternal life
column6: The final separation gives the two groups eternal punishment or eternal life, a Christian counterpart to the commentary's split between fire and the purified, praying person.

column5: The righteous beyond torment
column6: The righteous are in God's hand and no torment touches them, providing a Jewish wisdom contrast to the commentary's person destined for the great fire.

column5: Furnace of torment opposed to a place of rest
column6: The apocalyptic vision displays the furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest, a Jewish eschatological pairing for the commentary's fire and enduring differentiated outcome.

column5: Moses writes all the words of YHWH
column6: Moses writes the divine words after Sinai, a direct Torah antecedent for the commentary's closing appeal to Moses's early pages.

column5: The written book of the covenant read aloud
column6: Moses reads the book of the covenant to the people, bringing written pages together with recitation and hearing as in the commentary's preserved reminder.

column5: Moses completes writing Torah in a book
column6: The verse explicitly depicts Moses finishing the words of Torah in a book, the clearest canonical textual counterpart to Moses's pages in 87:19.

column5: Rabbinic attribution of Moses's book
column6: The Talmud's statement that Moses wrote his book is a Jewish reception of Mosaic textual authority relevant to the commentary's named pages of Moses.

column5: A restored corpus of revealed books
column6: Ezra's scribes complete ninety-four books after the law's loss, a Jewish apocalyptic meditation on preserving and differentiating former sacred writings.

column5: Abraham keeps charge, commandments, statutes, and laws
column6: Genesis attributes comprehensive obedience to Abraham, giving canonical footing for the commentary's Abrahamic former-scripture claim without assuming a canonical Abraham book.

column5: Abraham observed Torah before its giving
column6: The Talmud reads Genesis 26:5 as Abraham's fulfillment of the whole Torah before Sinai, a major Jewish interpretation beside the commentary's Abrahamic pages.

column5: Jesus says Moses wrote of him
column6: Jesus grounds his appeal in Moses's writing, a Christian interpretation of Mosaic pages that belongs beside the commentary's appeal to Moses as an earlier written authority.

column5: Scripture speaks beforehand to Abraham
column6: Paul personifies Scripture as announcing blessing beforehand to Abraham, a Christian rereading that makes Abraham a recipient of prior scriptural proclamation.

column5: Abraham's ancestors serve other gods
column6: Joshua locates Abraham's family beyond the river among worshippers of other gods, supplying canonical background for the commentary's Abrahamic plea to be kept from idols.

column5: God takes and leads Abraham
column6: God takes Abraham from beyond the river and leads him through Canaan, matching the commentary's Abrahamic selection and its wider path-and-guidance movement.

column5: Put away foreign gods and serve YHWH
column6: In the Abrahamic ancestral context Joshua calls Israel to remove foreign gods and serve YHWH, a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's avoidance of idols.

column5: Choose whom you will serve
column6: Joshua's demand to choose service of YHWH or other gods makes the commentary's preference theme concrete at the point of idolatry.

column5: Abraham's idol challenge and the furnace
column6: The midrash has Abraham reject idols and be cast into Nimrod's furnace, a Jewish expansion that tightly joins the commentary's Abrahamic anti-idolatry with its repeated fire scenes.

column5: Abraham obeys a call into an unknown destination
column6: Abraham obeys and goes out without knowing his destination, a Christian counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic trust, calling, and path imagery.

column5: A voice heard from the middle of fire
column6: Israel hears God's voice from fire but sees no form; this provides a wider Sinai form of the commentary's fire as a place of speech and revelation.

column5: The day and hour known only to the Father
column6: Jesus says the decisive day and hour are known to the Father alone, a close Christian analogue to the commentary's divinely concealed hour.

column5: Times and seasons fixed by the Father's authority
column6: Jesus withholds the times and seasons as the Father's own domain, complementing the commentary's hidden temporal decree without claiming the same formulation.

column5: A rite performed in remembrance
column6: Jesus commands the meal to be done in his remembrance; its explicit liturgical remembering is a Christian parallel to the commentary's fire-side prayer for remembrance.

column5: Magic books surrendered and burned
column6: Former practitioners publicly burn their magical books after confession, a later Christian scene of renouncing magic that complements the commentary's converted magicians without repeating its plot.

column5: A ruler aspiring to be like the Most High
column6: The arrogant ruler seeks equality with the Most High, a non-Pharaoh biblical analogue for the commentary's additional Pharaoh claim to supreme height.

column5: Lake of fire called the second death
column6: Revelation names the fiery lake the second death; its wording supplies a deliberate Christian contrast to the commentary's fire in which death and life are both denied.

column5: Faith tested as gold by fire
column6: The letter compares tested faith to gold proved by fire, a Christian refinement image for the commentary's corrective fire and enduring value.

column5: The rich person fading like grass's flower
column6: James uses scorched grass and fallen flower for the rich person's passing career, a specific Christian application of the commentary's worldly-life-as-drying-vegetation image.

column5: Restless waters casting up mud
column6: The wicked are like a turbulent sea that throws up mire, a related prophetic water-and-waste image beside the commentary's flood-borne scum; the material correspondence is indirect.

column5: Following the light on the way to life
column6: Jesus promises that followers of the world's light will not walk in darkness but have life's light; it is a Christian path-and-light counterpart to the commentary's fire sought for guidance.

column5: Cleansed bodies and drawing near in worship
column6: The faithful draw near with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed, joining purification and worship as the commentary joins tazkiya, name-remembrance, and prayer.

column5: Grace given according to measure
column6: Grace is given to each according to the measure of Christ's gift, a Christian individual-allotment image relevant to the commentary's move from measuring to portioning.

column5: A measure of faith allotted by God
column6: God assigns each person a measure of faith, supplying another specific Christian use of divinely apportioned measure beside the commentary's qadar imagery.

column5: Moses read in synagogues every Sabbath
column6: Acts describes Moses as publicly read in every city from ancient generations, a Christian witness to the continuing recitation of the Mosaic writings invoked by the commentary.

column5: The song of Moses as praise
column6: The heavenly worshippers sing the song of Moses in praise of God's great works, a Christian liturgical meeting of Moses, praise, and enduring divine rule.

column5: Receiving an unshakable kingdom and offering worship
column6: The community receives an unshakable kingdom and offers acceptable worship with awe, a Christian framing for the commentary's worship and permanence after transient life.

column5: Abraham and the priest of God Most High
column6: Hebrews names Melchizedek priest of God Most High in his encounter with Abraham, a Christian reuse of the highness title alongside Abraham; it is a title-and-scene meeting rather than a shared story.

column5: Abraham named God's friend and chosen lineage
column6: Isaiah calls Israel the offspring of Abraham God's friend and the chosen servant, supporting the commentary's pairing of Abraham, election, and earlier divine promise.

column5: Abraham's early confrontation with household idols
column6: The opening idol episodes are commonly cited for Abraham's testing and rejection of Terah's idols and fire-associated separation; the exact internal sequence should be verified, but it is a specific expansion of the commentary's anti-idolatry Abraham.

column4: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses II.20–21
column5: The unconsumed bush in Christian typology
column6: In the burning-bush interpretation commonly placed in these sections, Gregory reads the bush's non-consumption through later Christian typology; the section numbering should be checked, but it is a concrete reception of the fire detail central to the commentary.
